title: Assignment 3: ACS via tidycensus
text:
This page uses tidycensus to pull ACS 2024 5-year estimates for every county in Texas. It maps median household income and ranks counties by poverty rate, keeping the margin of error (MOE) next to every estimate in the table.
The deliverables from part 4 of the brief have their own headings below: 4a map, 4b table, 4c uncertainty check and 4d methods note. The code for each step is under “Show code”.

title: Assignment 3: ACS via tidycensus
text:
3. Download


Show code
# 4) Download, wide — one row per area, and the sf class survives
acs_wide <- get_acs(
  geography = geo_level,
  variables = my_vars,
  state     = state_abbr,
  year      = year_acs,
  survey    = survey,
  geometry  = TRUE,
  output    = "wide"
)

# 5) Derive a rate, and carry its margin of error through
acs_wide <- acs_wide |>
  mutate(pov_rate = povE / povdenE,
         pov_moe  = moe_prop(povE, povdenE, povM, povdenM))

  geom_sf(aes(fill = incomeE), color = "white", linewidth = 0.1) +
  scale_fill_viridis_c(name = "Median household income", labels = scales::label_dollar()) +
  labs(title = "Median household income by county, Texas",
       subtitle = paste0("ACS ", year_acs - 4, "–", year_acs, " 5-year estimates"),
       caption = "Source: U.S. Census Bureau via tidycensus") +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(text = element_text(family = "Palatino"),
        plot.title = element_text(size = 14, face = "bold"),
        plot.caption = element_text(size = 8),
        panel.grid = element_blank(),
        axis.text = element_blank(),

        legend.position.inside = c(0.2, 0.15))









Incomes are highest in the suburban counties around Dallas, Houston, Austin and San Antonio, like Collin, Denton, Fort Bend, Williamson and Kendall. Rockwall County is the highest at $127,981 (± $4,257). They are lowest in South Texas, along and near the border, like Starr, Zapata and Zavala, and in some small rural counties. Swisher County is the lowest at $36,165, but its MOE is ± $14,512. A few small rural counties also show up bright, like Glasscock at $101,250, but with an MOE of ± $53,302. The shading for small counties is much less certain than for the big metro counties.

title: Assignment 3: ACS via tidycensus
text:
4c. Uncertainty check
Dimmit County has the highest poverty rate in the table at 41.1% (± 8.9 points), so its 90% interval runs from 32.2% to 50.0%. Zapata County is second at 38.4% (± 6.0 points), from 32.4% to 44.4%. The two intervals overlap. Overlap is a rough check rather than a formal test, but here the gap between them is small next to both MOEs, so the data can’t tell us which county really has the higher rate. The table puts Dimmit County first, but a different sample could flip that order. The same is true for many other rows, especially small counties with wide MOEs, so the ranking is better read as high and low groups than as an exact order. Loving County is the extreme case: its 6.1% rests on 2 people out of 33, so its place in the table means very little.

title: Assignment 3: ACS via tidycensus
text:
4d. Methods note
I used counties because they cover all of Texas and most have samples large enough for usable estimates. Tracts would show more detail, but with much larger MOEs. I mapped median household income (B19013_001) and ranked counties by poverty rate: people below poverty (B17001_002) divided by the poverty universe (B17001_001), the people whose poverty status is determined. I used a rate because a count map mostly shows where people live, and I carried the rate’s MOE through with moe_prop() instead of dropping it.
The MOEs here are at the 90% confidence level, and they change how I read the results. Large counties have small MOEs, so their estimates are precise: Collin County is 6.2% ± 0.4 points. Small counties have small samples and wide MOEs: Edwards County is 31.9% ± 23.2 points and Foard County is 5.6% ± 4.4 points. Many counties at the top and bottom of the ranking are small ones like these, so the extremes are where the estimates are least reliable. When two 90% intervals don’t overlap I read the gap as real, and when they overlap I treat the order as uncertain.

text:
This page scrapes a practice site and two Wikipedia tables with rvest, cleans the foreign-exchange reserves table, and compares it with the same numbers from the World Bank API. It ends with a one-page plan for collecting web data for my own research. Answers are labeled with the question numbers from the assignment.

library(rvest)
library(dplyr)
library(stringr)
library(readr)
library(purrr)
library(ggplot2)
library(knitr)

options(HTTPUserAgent = "EPPS 6302 class assignment (UT Dallas)")

# save each page once, then read the saved copy
dir <- "data/webscrape"
dir.create(dir, showWarnings = FALSE, recursive = TRUE)

fetch <- function(url, file) {
  path <- file.path(dir, file)
  if (!file.exists(path)) {
    stopifnot(robotstxt::paths_allowed(url))   # check robots.txt first
    download.file(url, path, quiet = TRUE)
    Sys.sleep(2)                               # pause between requests
  }
  read_html(path)
}

    filter(!str_detect(country_or_region, regex("total|world", ignore_case = TRUE)))

clean_text <- function(x) {
  x |>
    str_replace_all("[\u2009\u202f\u00a0]", " ") |>   # thin and non-breaking spaces
    str_remove_all("\\[.*?\\]") |>                 # footnote markers like [1] or [note 2]
    str_remove_all("\\*") |>                       # the * the page adds after some names
    str_squish()
}

reserves <- reserves_raw |>
  # (ii) header spans three rows: set names, drop the two extra rows
  set_names(c("country", "continent", "incl_gold_musd", "incl_gold_change",
              "excl_gold_musd", "excl_gold_change", "last_reported", "ref")) |>
  filter(!country %in% names(reserves_raw)) |>
  mutate(across(everything(), clean_text)) |>
  # (ii) any Total or World row
  filter(!str_detect(country, regex("total|world", ignore_case = TRUE))) |>
  # (ii) drop the ref and change columns
  select(-ref, -incl_gold_change, -excl_gold_change) |>
  mutate(across(ends_with("_musd"), parse_number),
         # (i) dates come in several formats: "1 Mar 2024", "11 Sept 2026", "12 JUN 2026"
         date_text = last_reported,
         last_reported = lubridate::dmy(str_replace(last_reported, "\\bSept\\b", "Sep"), quiet = TRUE))

Which differ, and why. The largest holders mostly agree (China, South Korea, Singapore, Brazil and Saudi Arabia are within 4%), but many smaller countries do not. The gaps have five causes:

Different dates. 149 of the 196 Wikipedia rows are dated March 2024, while the World Bank value is mostly for the end of 2025. For Bolivia, Gabon and South Sudan, the Wikipedia numbers are close to their World Bank values for 2023, and the latest World Bank values are much lower (2025 for Bolivia, 2024 for the other two). Some World Bank series also stop early (Hong Kong after 2023, Afghanistan after 2020).
Gold valuation. The United States is 82% lower on Wikipedia. Its “including gold” figure is only about US$11 billion above “excluding gold”, which is US gold valued at the old official price of $42.22 an ounce. The World Bank uses the market price, which adds over US$1 trillion.
Coverage. The World Bank does not report Taiwan separately. Benin, Burkina Faso, Ivory Coast, Guinea-Bissau, Mali, Niger, Senegal and Togo share one central bank (the BCEAO), which holds their reserves together, so there is no World Bank figure for each country. Iran, North Korea, Cuba, Syria, Turkmenistan, Somalia, Andorra, Curaçao and Kiribati have no World Bank value for these years, and Vatican City and Montserrat are not in the World Bank’s country list.
Units. Mozambique and North Macedonia show 4 (US$ million) on Wikipedia but several billion at the World Bank. That looks like a number in billions entered in the millions column.
No checks. Nothing on Wikipedia checks the entries. “31 Apr 2024” and the unit errors are the mistakes visible here, and there is no way to tell how many others there are.

Which vintage. The World Bank numbers are end-of-year values, mostly for 2025, from the release updated on 2026-07-13. The Wikipedia numbers are from the page as I downloaded it on October 5, 2026, with reporting dates from March 2024 to September 2026. Scraping the page again next month could give different numbers, with no record of what changed.


3c. When is scraping the right tool?
Scraping is the right tool when the data is only published on a web page, with no API or download, and the site’s robots.txt and terms of service allow it. When the same numbers are available from an API or an official file, as the reserves are from the World Bank, use that instead, because it is documented, versioned and gives everyone the same answer.

title: Assignment 4: Webscraping 1
text:
4. Data plan
My research looks at how the timing of my coffee intake relates to my daily focus, using my own coffee log and a writing-time tracker. Web data gives an outside comparison: when people in the US search for coffee, by hour and day of the week. This shows whether my pattern matches the general one.
a. Source. Google Trends search interest for “coffee” in the US: hourly values for each 7-day window and daily values for the same three months as my logs. I chose it because it is the only free public source I found that shows coffee-related behavior by hour. The ICO and USDA publish coffee consumption only as yearly national totals, which cannot show a daily pattern. Coffee shop sales data would be closer to actual drinking, but it is not public.
b. robots.txt and Terms of Service. The robots.txt for trends.google.com blocks /explore? and /trends/explore?, the results pages a scraper would load. Google’s Terms of Service do not allow automated access that goes against robots.txt, so scraping those pages is not allowed. The gtrendsR package I used in Assignment 2 calls /trends/api/explore instead. robots.txt does not list that path, but it is not a public API: it has no documentation and Google can change or block it at any time. So I will not scrape Google Trends or use gtrendsR for this plan.
c. API. Google opened an official Trends API in July 2025, but only for approved applicants, and it gives daily, weekly, monthly or yearly data, not hourly. I will apply and use it for the daily series if I am approved. For the hourly data, and until then, I will use the “Download CSV” button on the Trends website. That is a person using the site, not a bot, so it follows robots.txt and the terms. Since I am not scraping, no justification is needed.
d. Volume, rate limiting and caching. About 13 hourly downloads (168 rows each) and one daily series over the three months, about 2,300 rows in total. Downloads are by hand, once a week, the same load as normal use. Google Trends is built from a sample, so the numbers can change between downloads (in Assignment 2 a repeat a few minutes later matched, but that does not prove they stay the same). I will save every file unchanged with the date in its name and log each download (search term, time window, download time). The analysis will only read the saved files.
e. What breaks, and how I will notice. Google can change the CSV layout (header lines or column names), how small values are shown (currently “<1”), or how the sample is drawn. A script will check each new file before I use it: the expected column names, 168 rows for a 7-day hourly file, values between 0 and 100 with a top value of 100, and dates that match the window I asked for. If a check fails, the script stops and names the file.

Part A is the download_govfiles_pdf() function from govtdata01.R, run on the pdfLink column of my export. My copy of the script has no Part B, so I wrote it with httr2 from section 2: it takes the ten newest from the API search in 2b and fetches each from /packages/{packageId}/pdf. Both wait 1 to 3 seconds between files.

api_top10    <- api_all |> slice_head(n = 10) |> mutate(rank = row_number())
export_top10 <- export  |> slice_head(n = 10) |> mutate(rank = row_number())

log_file <- file.path(dir, "download_log.csv")

# Part A: the function from govtdata01.R
save_dir <- paste0(pdf_dir, "/")
download_govfiles_pdf <- function(url, id) {
  tryCatch({
    destfile <- paste0(save_dir, "govfiles_", id, ".pdf")
    download.file(url, destfile = destfile, mode = "wb") # Binary files
    Sys.sleep(runif(1, 1, 3))
    return(paste("Successfully downloaded:", url))
  },
  error = function(e) {
    return(paste("Failed to download:", url))
  })
}

# Part B: one package at a time from the API
download_api_pdf <- function(id) {
  destfile <- file.path(pdf_dir, paste0("api_", id, ".pdf"))
  resp <- govinfo(paste0("packages/", id, "/pdf")) |>
    req_error(is_error = \(r) FALSE) |>
    req_perform(path = destfile)
  Sys.sleep(runif(1, 1, 3))
  paste("HTTP", resp_status(resp))
}

# one log row per file, with the time it finished
log_row <- function(method, attempt, rank, id, url, file, result) {
  tibble(method, attempt, rank, packageId = id, url, file, result,
         bytes = file.size(file), md5 = unname(tools::md5sum(file)),
         finished = format(Sys.time(), "%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S %Z", tz = "America/Chicago"))
}

run_a <- function(rows, attempt) {
  pmap(list(rows$rank, rows$packageId, rows$pdfLink), \(rank, id, url) {
    result <- download_govfiles_pdf(url, id)
    log_row("A: export + download.file()", attempt, rank, id, url,
            paste0(save_dir, "govfiles_", id, ".pdf"), result)
  }) |> list_rbind()
}

The dataset has 14,520 tweets from November 7 to November 16, 2021 (UTC). 62% are retweets and 93% are in English. Frequent words. Stopwords, URLs, hashtags and mentions are removed here; they get their own networks below.

A CPD document is not all the President’s words. Transcripts label each turn (“The President.”, “Q.” for a reporter, “Secretary Rubio.”, “President Xi.”). The OFR editors add subject headings inside transcripts (“China-U.S. Trade”), bracketed notes (“[Laughter]”), and at the end a note, categories, and an index of the names mentioned. So I split each document into the president’s words, other speakers, and the editors’ text. The speaker labels are found with a regular expression. It is a heuristic: a few paragraphs that start with a name, like a list of companies, are taken as another speaker.


Show code
# transcripts label each turn ("The President.", "Q.", "Secretary Rubio."); a paragraph
# without a label continues the last speaker, and an unlabeled document is all the president's
president_re <- "^(The President|President Biden|President Trump)\\. "
reporter_re  <- "^Q\\. "
word_re      <- "(?:(?:Mr|Mrs|Ms|Dr|Lt|Col|Capt|Maj|Gen|Sen|Rep|Gov|Comd|U\\.S)\\.|[A-Z][A-Za-z'’-]*|of|de|da|la|bin)"
other_re     <- paste0("^(?!(?:And|But|So|Alright|Okay|Well|Yes|No|Now|Oh|On|Go|Happy|That.s|Thank|Thanks|Good|Great|Right)\\b)",
                       "(?:", word_re, " ){1,5}[A-Z][A-Za-z'’-]+\\. ")

label_turns <- function(paras) {
  # a few paragraphs hold more than one turn
  paras <- unlist(str_split(paras, "\\s(?=(?:Q|The President|President Biden|President Trump)\\. )"))
  # the editors add subject headings ("China-U.S. Trade") and bracketed notes ("[Laughter]")
  heading <- nchar(paras) < 120 & !str_detect(paras, "[.?!:;,—–\"”’)…\\]]$")
  bracket <- str_extract_all(paras, "\\[[^\\]]*\\]") |> map_chr(\(x) paste(x, collapse = " "))
  text    <- str_squish(str_remove_all(paras, "\\[[^\\]]*\\]"))
  speaker <- case_when(heading ~ "heading",
                       str_detect(text, president_re) ~ "president",
                       str_detect(text, reporter_re)  ~ "reporter",
                       str_detect(text, other_re)     ~ "other",
                       .default = NA_character_)
  last <- "president"
  for (i in seq_along(speaker)) {
    if (is.na(speaker[i])) speaker[i] <- last
    if (speaker[i] != "heading") last <- speaker[i]
  }
  tibble(speaker, text = if_else(heading, paras, str_remove(text, president_re)), bracket)
}

# split each document into the president's words, other speakers, and what the OFR editors added
split_cpd <- function(file) {
  paras <- read_html(file) |> html_elements("p, h1") |> html_text2() |> str_squish()
  paras <- paras[paras != ""]
  end   <- detect_index(paras, \(p) str_detect(p, "^(\\[Filed|NOTE:|Categories:|Names:|Subjects:|DCPD Number:)"))
  if (end == 0) end <- length(paras) + 1
  # administration line, title, and the date line when there is one
  n_head <- if (str_detect(paras[3], paste0("^(", paste(month.name, collapse = "|"), ") \\d"))) 3 else 2
  turns  <- label_turns(paras[seq_len(end - 1)][-seq_len(n_head)])
  join   <- \(x) paste(x[x != ""], collapse = "\n")
  tibble(header          = paste(head(paras, n_head), collapse = " | "),
         president_words = join(turns$text[turns$speaker == "president"]),
         others          = join(turns$text[turns$speaker %in% c("reporter", "other")]),
         editors         = join(c(turns$text[turns$speaker == "heading"], turns$bracket,
                                  paras[seq_along(paras) >= end])))
}

title: Assignment 6: Text analytics with quanteda
text:
4. Report
Two kinds of text (2a.iii). The tweets show what people on Twitter passed around during the summit week, and most of it was the news. 62% are retweets, and many repeat quotes from the opening remarks in the CPD transcript: “old friend” (1,197 tweets), “guardrails” (304), “rules of the road” (277). The hashtags and mentions add what the official text leaves out: COVID, fentanyl, Taiwan, and activists urging Biden to raise the Uyghurs and Tibet. The tweets cannot say what was agreed, and they are not a sample of the public. They were written by accounts that used the collector’s keywords in that window, for their followers.
The CPD has the President’s public words as spoken. For the summit it has one document, the remarks before the closed talks. Over five years it shows how each White House talked about China. Biden says “Xi Jinping” and retells his personal history with him. Trump says “President Xi” and talks about a great relationship, deals and tariffs. The White House produced these texts for the press and the public record, and the OFR edited them. They show how the presidents presented policy in public. They do not show how it was made. The 2025 YouTube comments were written by viewers of a few news videos, for other viewers, and are more about Trump than about China.
Data-generating processes. The tweets were chosen by a keyword and a collection window. So the frequent words and LSA describe what spread among those accounts, mostly retweets of a few posts. The CPD documents were chosen first by the White House (what it released), then by an OFR editor (what goes in, plus headings, notes and an index of names), and then by my query. The query matches that index, so 12 documents are in the corpus only because an editor listed Xi. The keyness compares what each White House released, including Trump’s long press exchanges (787,645 words in 160 documents against 488,544 in 175). So it compares two ways of talking in public. It says little about the two China policies. The inaugurals were chosen by tradition: one speech per term, the same occasion, written for the nation. The 21 speeches are all there is, so differences between them come from the year and the speaker. With only 21, party keyness is weak.
What Wordfish measures (3b). Wordfish (Slapin and Proksch 2008) assumes each word count in a speech is drawn from a Poisson distribution, with a rate set by the speech’s length, the word’s overall frequency, and the speech’s position on one hidden dimension times the word’s weight on it. Words are independent of each other and their order is ignored. On the inaugurals the dimension seems to measure time. It correlates 0.87 with the year, and party adds nothing. Postwar words (“peoples”, “resources”, “program”, “equality”) are at one end; “thank”, “everyone”, “borders”, “jobs” and “protect” are at the other. It could be the policy words of each era, or a change from formal to direct speech. To show what it measures I would need outside evidence: correlation with an independent measure (such as hand-coded tone or expert ideology scores), stable results when I change the preprocessing, and the same dimension found within one era. I must set dir because the model is identified only up to its sign. Flipping every position and word weight fits the data equally well. dir = c(Truman 1949, Trump 2025) puts Truman below Trump, so later speeches are on the positive side. Without it, the direction is arbitrary.

Source. Compilation of Presidential Documents (collection CPD), published by the Office of the Federal Register, National Archives and Records Administration, on GovInfo. Accessed through the GovInfo API (api.govinfo.gov): /search, /packages/{id}/summary and /packages/{id}/htm.
Permission. Works of the US government are in the public domain (17 U.S.C. § 105). The API needs a free api.data.gov key. I waited 1 to 2 seconds between downloads, well under the rate limit.
Query. collection:(CPD) AND “Xi Jinping” AND publishdate:range(2021-01-20,), sorted by publish date, paged 100 at a time, run on 2026-10-19 07:50:57 CDT.
Selection. The search returned 344 packages, all downloaded (HTTP 200). I excluded the 9 annual digests and checklists, leaving 335 documents: 175 from Biden and 160 from Trump. The administration comes from each package’s president field. Text analysis uses only the president’s words, split from other speakers and from editors’ headings, brackets and notes with the regular expressions above.
Gaps. The search matches the editors’ index of names, so 12 documents are included only because the editors list Xi, and in 41 more only a reporter or another leader says his name. A document where the President says only “Xi” and the editors do not list the full name could be missed. There are no results between January 20 and March 17, 2021, although Biden called Xi on February 10, 2021. That call appears only as a line in the 2021 Digest, not as a document of its own. The latest document is from 2026-09-12, so the CPD seems to run a few weeks behind, and there is no 2025 Digest yet. Translated remarks by foreign leaders and reporters’ questions are in the documents but not in my analysis. The speaker split is a heuristic.

2a–b. Dates and interval. The five-year file runs weekly from September 26, 2021 to September 27, 2026 (262 weeks). The 90-day file runs daily from June 29, 2026 to September 29, 2026 (93 days), so the interval changes with the window. In both, the last week or day was still in progress when I pulled it.
2c. Units. These are not search counts. Each point is a share of all searches in that place and time, rescaled so the highest point in the query is 100. A 0 means the volume was too low to show, and “<1” means some interest but under 1 (Google).
2d. Removing a term. With Election dropped, the other two terms changed. Trump’s top value went from 26 to 100, and none of its 262 weeks kept the same number. Kamala Harris’s top value went from 7 to 26, and only 228 of 262 weeks stayed the same, all of them “<1” weeks. Election’s spike had set the 100, so without it everything was rescaled. The numbers only compare within one query.
1d. My own term. “USA Iran war” peaks the week of March 1, 2026. Outside March 2026, its biggest spike is 51 the week of June 22, 2025, around the US strikes on Iranian nuclear sites. It is 0 in 121 of 262 weeks, 102 of them before 2025, and has been above zero every week since January 2026. It only counts searches with all three words, so it misses people who typed “Iran war”.

4. Comparing the two methods


Show code
web_long <- web1 |> mutate(keyword = recode(keyword, Election = "election")) |> rename(web = hits)
r_long <- r_match$interest_over_time |>
  transmute(date = as.Date(date), keyword, r = as.character(hits))
both <- inner_join(web_long, r_long, by = c("date", "keyword"))
first_long <- r_first$interest_over_time |> transmute(date = as.Date(date), keyword, r = as.character(hits))
script_match <- inner_join(web_long, first_long, by = c("date", "keyword"))
# script's Harris against the website's Kamala Harris, week by week
harris <- inner_join(filter(web_long, keyword == "Kamala Harris"), filter(first_long, keyword == "Harris"), by = "date") |>
  mutate(web = num(web), r = num(r))

t_first  <- max(r_log$pulled_utc[r_log$name == "trump_harris_election_us_5y" & r_log$ok])
t_repeat <- r_log$pulled_utc[r_log$name == "trump_harris_election_us_5y_repeat2"]
gap_min  <- round(as.numeric(difftime(t_repeat, t_first, units = "mins")))




Show code
ggplot(both, aes(date)) +
  geom_line(aes(y = num(web), color = "Website CSV")) +
  geom_point(aes(y = num(r), color = "gtrendsR"), size = 0.6) +
  facet_wrap(~ keyword, ncol = 3) +
  labs(title = "Same query two ways: Trump, Kamala Harris, election",
       subtitle = "gtrendsR points sit exactly on the website line",
       caption = "\"<1\" plotted as 0.5",
       x = NULL, y = "Interest (0-100)", color = NULL) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(legend.position = "top")









4a. Are the numbers identical? Yes. I ran the exact website query in R (Kamala Harris, not Harris), and all 786 of 786 values match, with no gap in either direction. The script’s own query with “Harris” also matches the website exactly for Trump (262 of 262) and election (262 of 262), because election’s spike sets the 100 in both. Only the Harris column differs, and it is higher than the website’s Kamala Harris in 262 of 262 weeks. Most weeks it is 1 where Kamala Harris is <1, and it peaks at 11 against 7.
4b(i). Reproducibility. Neither method lets someone else regenerate my file exactly. “Past 5 years” is a moving window, so the same settings cover different weeks tomorrow, and Trends is built from a sample. The R code makes re-running easy, but only my cached files hold these exact numbers.
4b(ii). Provenance. R records the query for me: every row carries the keyword, geography, window, search type and category. It does not record when it ran, and “today+5-y” does not say which five years, so I logged the pull times myself. The website CSV notes the terms, the geography, the category and that the values are weekly. It does not note the time window setting, the search type or when I downloaded it, so I wrote those down in the datasheet.
4b(iii). Scale. Both allow five terms per query. Fifty terms means at least ten separate searches, each on its own 0-100 scale. In R that is a loop, but the rescaling problem stays, and fifty requests run into rate limits.
4b(iv). Fragility. gtrendsR scrapes a service with no general public API. Of my first nine calls, 3 failed and worked a few minutes later. I knew because R threw an error. If Google quietly changed its scaling, nothing would error. On the website, a wrong setting or a changed page layout only gets caught if every choice was recorded.
4c. Same call twice. When I ran the first call again 4 minutes later, it returned the same numbers, 786 of 786 values, so Google appears to reuse the same sample over a short window. That does not prove the data is stable. Trends is a sample, and my test only covered a few minutes. Every finding from this source needs its exact query and pull time, and should come from a saved file, not a fresh call.

title: Assignment 1: Designing My Website
text:
This website is created using RStudio Quarto. It is a Quarto website project where each page is a .qmd file, and the _quarto.yml file sets the title, theme and navigation bar. When the site is rendered, Quarto builds the pages into the docs folder, and GitHub Pages publishes them from there.
The Cosmo theme is used for a professional look. It is clean and easy to read, with a white background, a light navigation bar and blue links. There is also a styles.css file in case I want to change the look later, and the table of contents is turned on so pages with sections show a list of them on the right.
The navigation bar includes four links connecting to my content in different areas. Home is the welcome page. Research describes my project on coffee consumption and daily productivity cycles. CV has my curriculum vitae. Assignments is a drop-down menu for my EPPS 6302 coursework, and this note is under Assignment 1. I used a drop-down for assignments so the navigation bar doesn’t get crowded as more assignments are added during the semester. The site title on the left goes back to the home page, and the search icon on the right searches the whole site.
I kept the design simple. Every page uses the same theme and navigation bar, so the site looks the same throughout and is easy to move around.
The website is hosted on GitHub Pages from my repository tynshanaboone.github.io, and it is live at https://tynshanaboone.github.io. When I update a page, I render the site again in RStudio and send the updated files to GitHub.
